text.p: Sweden's state-controlled Norbanken was in the financial spotlight on Friday after a newspaper report added weight to months of speculation over a merger with another major bank, S-E-Banken.

Business daily Dagens Industri reported that the government was expected to sell 20-25 percent of its 58 percent stake of Nordbanken to Investor AB, the investment vehicle of Sweden's leading finance family, the Wallenbergs.
The paper said this deal would pave the way for Nordbanken to merge with S-E-Banken as the Wallenberg dynasty owns 15 percent of the bank's capital and 16 percent of votes.
Analysts saw Investor buying into Nordbanken as feasible.
"It is a simple and neat solution," one Stockholm analyst told Reuters.
However others voiced some hesitancy about the accuracy of the information given by sources to Dagens Industri.
"It provides one of several possible solutions to solve the ownership problem," Goran Kallebo, an analyst at Matteus brokerage, told Reuters.
Although the government has said it intends to divest its stake in Nordbanken, the report in Dagens Industri was quickly denied by the government.
"The state is not taking part in any negotiations concerning Nordbanken," Finance Minister Erik Asbrink's spokeswoman Anna Forsberg told Reuters.
Investor spokesman Nils-Ingvar Lundin said it was company policy not to comment on any market rumours or speculation.
But analysts saw Investor as a possible Nordbanken suitor.
"Investor has nearly no loans and could borrow 25 billion crowns ($3.63 billion) to buy the entire state stake, giving the Wallenbergs about a third of the new (merged) bank," an analyst said.
"Then Investor could redeem shares for five billion crowns or so to boost the value of the new bank and to get money to invest in IT companies (which it has said it intends to do)."
Despite the denials, Nordbanken shares surged when the Stockholm bourse opened, jumping 14.5 crowns to 230 crowns before slipping back to 224.5 crowns at 1215 GMT.
Speculation about Nordbanken and S-E-Banken has been in the market for months and driven Nordbanken's share price up by 70 percent since early September.
In November Asbrink flatly denied comments by Bertil Aberg, head of Sweden's largest mortgage lender Stadshypotek, that the government was thinking of selling its Nordbanken stake to S-E-Banken.
Asbrink said the action plan was for the state to first sell its holding in Stadshypotek.
But the sale of Stadshypotek is now out of the way

Handelsbanken, Sweden's largest bank by assets, in December made a 22.9 billion cash takeover bid for the Stadshypotek, of which the state owns 34 percent, which has government approval and looks set to proceed.
Since then Nordbanken and S-E-Banken merger rumours have re-emerged as part of the market expectations of a major restructuring in Sweden's finance sector.

A merger of Nordbanken and S-E-Banken, with market capitalisations of 38.2 billion crowns and 36.1 billion crowns respectively, would create a huge bank able to compete with other large European banks seen entering Sweden after 1999.
The banks would be complementary. Nordbanken focuses on private customers and small companies while S-E-Banken is strong in large company deals and investment banking.
Elsewhere, analysts are keeping a close eye on the fourth of Sweden's major banks, Swedbank, which is considered a potential suitor for Foreningsbanken.
($1=6.884 Swedish Crown)
